properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-29 during the v0.43.0 cut. PR #385 shipped `cap:a-client-elects-a-server-of-its-own-build` with a PASSING Verification but no `ALLOCATED_TO` and no `REALIZES` — a capability with a check, no owning part and no file. Its CI was green and correctly so: the two gaps it raises score 0.50 ("isn't assigned to any part") and 0.45 ("nothing builds it"), and `reflow2_check.py --gap-threshold` defaults to 0.80. The gate exited 0 with both listed as NOTES.

THE DEBT SURFACED ONE PR LATER, in the release cut, and only because a human READ the notes. That is the asymmetry worth naming: CI reads the EXIT CODE, and a person reads the OUTPUT. Everything between 0.00 and 0.80 is visible to exactly one of those two readers, and nothing routes it to the other.

WHAT THIS IS NOT: a calibration error. 0.80 is a defensible line and lowering it to 0.45 would fail the build on every deliberately-deferred allocation (`dec:idea-allocation-waits-for-the-last-responsible-moment` parks exactly that, on purpose). The observation is narrower and it is about AGE: severity is computed from the gap's shape, and knows nothing about whether the capability was introduced by the commit under test or has stood unallocated for six weeks. A brand-new orphan and a long-accepted deferral score identically. The FIRST is a thing the author forgot in the last hour and would fix on sight; the SECOND is a standing decision. Only the author of the PR can tell them apart, and they are the one reader the exit code never shows the list to.

NOT PROPOSING A FIX. `loop_status {"since_export": true}` already computes what is owed on ground the committed export does not hold, which is the closest existing answer to "what did THIS change introduce" — whether the gate should use it is undecided and nobody has been asked.
